# Serum 2 - Practitioner Videos + Online Guide: Workflow Digest

Source set for the Anvil GUI/workflow redesign study (private design reference only; not for redistribution).

## Method / Evidence trail

- PART 1 videos: "Complete Guide To Master Serum 2" YouTube playlist (14 videos). Auto-caption subtitles fetched with yt-dlp (2026.08.19) as VTT into raw/subs/, de-duplicated into readable text in text/video-subs/, and digested below. All 14 videos yielded captions: 12 on the first pass; lOZ56pKhTqU and iF8cm3RmVmQ first hit HTTP 429 rate limiting on the 'en' subtitle track and were captured later on the 'en-orig' track. Quotes are the presenter's words via auto-captions; capitalization/obvious ASR slips cleaned, otherwise kept as heard.
- PART 2 guide: https://www.edmprod.com/serum-2-guide/ fetched with curl (UA Mozilla/5.0) into raw/guide.html; article text extracted to text/guide.txt; digested below.
- PART 3 frames: 3 videos downloaded at <=480p into cache/serum2-videos/ (VPfqZq7EpNY 93.4 MB / 2876 s; FxmpF24EUYE 57.2 MB / 1469 s; D2GB6bGy-Nw 29.6 MB / 827 s; durations verified with ffprobe). Frames: 1 per 60 s at 640 px wide -> frames/<id>/ (48 / 24 / 14 PNG). Numbered contact sheets: 5x4 tiles at 480 px -> frames/<id>-sheet-N.png (6 sheets). Best-of sheets (hand-picked full-UI frames): frames/<id>-bestof.png (3 sheets). See Part 3 for the full inventory.
- Same tree, separate workstream (left untouched): raw/manual/ + raw/scripts/ + raw/text/ hold a Serum manual scrape.
- Limits: auto-captions carry ASR errors (product terminology near-perfect, names occasionally garbled); frame samples are 1/minute and not scene-accurate.

## PART 1 - Video digests (Complete Guide To Master Serum 2, by Evil Sounds)

Format notes: the presenter structures the series as "blocks" plus a hands-on "sound design sesh" at the end of each episode that may only use blocks covered so far; later episodes deliberately combine earlier blocks. Quotes are from auto-captions (lightly cleaned).

### EP1 - "Wavetable Oscillator" (VPfqZq7EpNY, 48 min) - subs OK
Series frame: "I want to make this one into little blocks that we can kind of go through together. And as we finish each block, we will have a sound design sesh at the end where we will only be allowed to use what we have covered so far."
UI areas used: the wavetable oscillator panel (Osc A/B); wavetable display as a menu entry point; unison strip under the wavetable; phase section; pitch section (octave/semi/fine/coarse); pan; the warp row; sub oscillator (left side); noise section.
- Order of operations taught: (1) open the wavetable CATEGORY MENU by clicking the wavetable display region - categories Analog, Digital, Spectral, User; User is "where you can install your wavetables"; (2) pick a starting tone; (3) optionally use it as a static "color selector / tone selector" - "I'm using the wavetable more as a color selector... I can select a point in time"; (4) shape with unison, phase, pitch, warps; (5) add sub oscillator then noise last.
- Interaction specifics: clicking the wavetable opens the category menu; right-click menus exist (right-click the pitch "mode" control -> Harmonics or Ratio); alt+drag observed ("I'm holding alt and moving"); knobs are drag; the phase section has an expander arrow revealing Continuous and Phase memory modes.
- Pro/crucial callouts: unison MODE section is "a part that probably 95% of people that use serum don't ever go into" (linear vs super vs stack changes voice behavior); "with odd numbers you have one center voice... if I wanted to create a sound that is monocompatible or a bass sound, I would go for an odd number"; phase/random settings are crucial for basses ("people don't put the time to get the phase right"; random=0 activates "a re-trig"); the pitch secret menu (right-click mode -> harmonics) is "a secret menu, which again 95% of people won't even bother with"; pan-per-oscillator is "clutch... super slept on by many people" for organic width vs the unison way; Serum 2's new oscillator-jnternal Filter warp lets you stack layers that "respect the space of each other"; the new Distortion warp folds/shapes the waveform in place ("this is how you do it" for fold-style wavetables).
- Wrap-up quote: "if you're like me and you just get straight to work without reading the manual, you can definitely miss them" (hidden features).
- Deliberately deferred: FM and phase distortion ("we're going to talk about in a separate video"), multisample/sample/granular/spectral (next episode).

### EP2 - "Multisample and Sampler" (Jgg-dOhBLqk, 31 min) - subs OK
- Recap additions to EP1: right-click the Wavetable Position knob -> "create smooth interpolation" (smooth crossfade between frames so scanning "moves" smoothly); switch pitch tracking off to play any key at fixed pitch (drone/atmosphere sound design).
- Access pattern for the new oscillator engines: "to access these new features, you just click on the wave table and then you get the submenu where you can dive into these guys" - the wavetable display is a dropdown that switches the oscillator between Wavetable / Multisample / Sample (Granular and Spectral follow in EP3). This is the same click-point used in EP1 to open the wavetable category browser.
- Multisample: sample-map instrument playable across the keyboard. Requires a mapping script file (he calls it "a sfc [sfz]... a text file... to let Serum know what notes pertain to what sample"); he generated his with ChatGPT. Factory library is velocity-layered ("this SFC file is velocity sensitive" - soft/hard hits are different samples). Controls: pitch (as wavetable), envelope override ("you can override the envelope that the original creator... inputed"; "usually I won't override it, though, unless it's needed for sound design purposes"), velocity track, rand (start-point randomization), timbre (reorders which samples play - can brighten, but "sounds a little bit unnatural"), unison + width/range/stack/warp.
- Sample (single-sample) mode: start/end markers; loop modes One shot / Forward / Reverse / Forward-Reverse / a "Tail" mode; right-click ON THE SAMPLE WR A VEFORM menu: normalize, reverse, trim; slicing Auto and Manual ("similar to Ableton's Simpler slice mode"), Option/Alt+click to add or remove slice markers, "Play slice to end", "Set root note", and right-click "Send to selected clip" (sends the slice into the Clip Sequencer); scan rate (playback speed, negative = reverse) with "Lock scan rate to tempo" and "Lock sample to BPM" (sizes: 1 bar, 1/2...).
- Hidden/second-layer controls behind right-click: "relative loop", "link loop length" (with right-click "Show marker animation" to visualize), "exit loop on release"; on start/end markers: "Snap to zero / Snap to beat / Snap to loop"; there is also a crossfade control that smooths forward-reverse loops ("you can't even tell").
- Sample-mode unison extras: voice start-position offset ("each start at different positions of the sample... unique to just the sample - the multi-sample doesn't let you do that") and "span" to localize the center point; plus the same phase/stack controls as wavetable.
- Workflow session (layering doctrine): combine organic + inorganic - multisample bass guitar for tone at C3 keyboard range, then Osc B basic shape (sine/triangle) dropped -3 octaves "to beef it up... use as a bass for a house track"; grand piano + wavetable layer + LP filter; marimba/mallet layers; then switching to Sample mode "so I can loop the piano and get a really nice reverse". Layering principle: "when I'm layering sounds, I'm trying to fill in something that might be missing from the other one."
- Flow quote: "When you know your tools and you get comfortable and you know everything you can do... then you can stay in flow. Move fast."
- Flavor quote: "Serum 2 went from being a synth to a super synth in a sense, and a super sampler."

### EP3 - "Granular & Spectral" (Z55OQxV6zfA, 28 min) - subs OK
- Framing: "these are going to be the most CPU intensive sections of Serum 2... break new sonic boundaries, create atmospheres, create glitch-like effects, create cool tech house effects, dubstep wobbles."
- Granular concepts: any sound source is split into grains. Length = grain size ("if you have a short length you're going to have a lot of grains"); Density = how many grains play at the same time (with density 1 it behaves like a sampler; "actually what starts to change is once we start to move this density"). Randomization layer over each grain: Random Length, Random Pitch (semitones), Random Pan, Random Scan/start point, volume, direction (forward/reverse), and offset ("we can modulate when each one starts, where, if it's pan left or right. We can randomize that. We can randomize the volume... the pitch... the direction").
- Crossfade ("this blue here") controls blending between grains: amount + shape + skew, with its own randomize per value.
- Unison per grain: "we can unison each grain. And this is what makes it so CPU intensive because the moment I increase this, each grain is getting detuned"; settings mirror wavetable unison (blend, detune, stack, start, span, range, width, mono) plus a Spawn Pattern: all together / even / exponential ("one spawns in a second, the next one's going to spawn in two, and then in four, and then in eight") / random.
- Signature interaction (important for GUI): right-click on the grain display -> "Show XY controller" - the XY dot can control sample position, and a second right-click assigns what the Y axis controls (volume / warp / grain length); can also be added to a macro.
- BPM sync: density/length can be set in note divisions ("every one fourth, there's a grain... dotted"), and sample utilities are right-click menus ("I can right click and normalize it", trim).
- Spectral concepts: "with spectral we're manipulating the frequency itself, not the shape of a wave"; display shows frequency content (green intensity = harmonic content; bottom = low, top = high); a region selector on the display works "almost like a filter... to cut out certain parts"; new Cut/filter section over the harmonics ("we can alter the frequencies, the harmonics of the sound, and move to create these nasty ass things") with remap drawing and presets; you can even load a wavetable into the spectral display ("you can also click here and put a wave table... which is very interesting. I don't know how I would use that, but just found out with you guys").
- Spectral Warp list (new in Serum 2, not in the manual per presenter): Smear (blurs transients), Spread +/- (spreads harmonics across spectrum), Harmonics, Subharmonics (adds below - "think of it as almost like a sub oscillator"), Gate (gates out quieter frequencies), Robotize, Shift, Mirror, Peak follow, Peak octave +/-12, Peak harmonics +/-12, Harm sweep, Shepard / Shepard W (ever-rising illusion tone), Comb, Pitch blend, Pitch shift, Phase shift, Formant (vocal A / OY qualities), Mask ("you're going to need something in Sounds of Space or C to use"), Vocoder.
- Sound design session: spectral strings stab + subharmonics, add a reese via another osc, LP filter, fine tune, warp, Spread, then "let's get that 3D effect on the sound by respecting the space and widening this"; a kick loop at low pitch as texture; granular vocal ("Take your medicine, honey") mangled into glitch/stutter.
- Quotes: "As granular, you have to hear it in order to understand what you can do with it."; "If someone asked me to remake this sound just using a synth, it would be really hard."

### EP4 - "Filters" (uqQB_kC53yo, 43 min) - subs OK
- Framing: "we're talking about filters, which is all about manipulating the frequency of the sound you've created in your oscillator section"; later: "Filters are probably one of the biggest backbones of sound design. Probably one of the most important things. And each filter is different... don't get caught in the trap of every low pass filter is the same. It's not."
- UI: two filter units (Filter 1 / Filter 2); each opens a tab menu with sub-menus: "Normal, Multi, Flange, Misc, and Serum 2 filters"; Normal = "the bread and butter filters... the most used filters."
- Controls taught in order: Cutoff ("where the removal of the frequency starts"); Resonance (boost at cutoff; warned that "when you increase the resonance you are losing a bit of low end"); Drive (pushes level into the filter - rounding/squaring into saturation produces harmonics, compression, warmth, fattiness); Fat ("brings [low end] back up... more focused on this resonance point"); Pan ("one of the most underused sections in Serum 2's filter range" - it "changes the value of the cutoff for the left and right signal" so a mono sound gains width); Mix (dry/wet amount; he says the mix knob becomes valuable with the more extreme filters).
- Routing sounds into filters: "I need to input and let Serum know that I want oscillator B or C to come in... clicking here. When it's highlighted blue, it's telling Serum that the sound is being allowed through." Per-oscillator routing can send to filter 1 only, filter 2 only, both at once (parallel), or in series F1 -> F2 ("it goes into filter one and then filter two and then it goes into the effects... we can change the signal flow as well"). There is also a routing selector at the top right of the oscillator section ("there's this M... If I route that to A... now here is where you control the filter balance. We can route it to filter two, filter one, or we can have both one and two working at the same time on the same sound in parallel").
- Slope number (dB pole): "when we use a higher number it's more strict and when we use a lower number it's less strict. More highs are allowed out" (6 / 12 / 18 / 24); a warm punchy bass wants the steeper LP; "the flavor of the filter matters... that's the character of the filter, the tonality of it."
- Key track: "if I'm playing a low octave bass... when I decide to play higher up, you can barely feel or hear that... key track makes it so that those high notes become more audible and more present" - recommended whenever a sound "can be played as a bass, as a lead or a sound that covers a whole range."
- Filter families walked through, in order: Normal LP (incl. MG variants - "the thing that changes is the way this resonance works"), HP, BP ("like the low pass and high pass had a baby"), Peak, Notch; then Multi section combining filters (LH6 = low+high pass together; LB12 = LP+BP; LP+Peak; morphable filters "where the game changes a bit because these guys are morphable... we can morph between the filters like this... useful again for movement on the sound, like a pad. Imagine now the cutoff moving as well"); Flange section (combs = notches+boosts altering phase; flange; phasers; formant phaser "for wubs" - with the note "you always will lose power and you will always lose a bit of presence, but in return... that interesting tone"); Misc/Mix section (EQ-style filters; Ring Mod and Ring Mod x2 with Spread - "for adding an interesting tone... R2D2" plus mix knob; Sample & Hold - bitcrush, "Josh Baker Chris Stussy stuff"; Reverb/Allpass/Comb - "smear the sound"; French LP and German LP - differently flavored LPs with "squelchy" response; Add bass - per manual "phase rotated low pass filter with a touch of drive"; Formant filters - vocal "hey yo" quality; Band Reject - "opposite of a band pass" with width + resonance = "the devil's horns"; Comb LP/BP/Comb 2 - positive/negative combs; Scream filters - "screech-like quality... the magic happens when the drive starts going above a certain amount... very Prodigy"); Serum 2 filters (Wasp; morph; DJ mixer; diffuser; stages; MG ladder = Moog-style, "smoother... not going to be as bitey"; PCSBF - "you can draw in your filters... create almost like your own filter wave table" with presets and switching/modulation between them; Comb 2; ExpMm = "multi-mode LPF notch HPF... from the classic synthesizer expander module").
- Interactions: click the filter name to open the filter list; right-click or "alt click" the filter response graph "to switch between the modes... to see what the filter does to the sound" including phase display ("the more harsh the cut... the more it's going to affect the phases").
- Workflow session recipes: (1) parallel-filter pad - one osc routed into F1 (flange) and F2 (phaser) at once, "both are going to go directly to the master"; (2) serial bass chain - spectral oscillator into F1 high pass (removing its low end) then F2 low pass, with the saw routed only into F2 so "the tonality of this guy [spectral layer] controls the high end... the saw will still provide that fatness" (a formula for "unique basses"); (3) tech house lead - F1 LP at 6 dB with filter one routed to filter two, F2 = sample & hold, high resonance, key track on.
- Homework list he gives: "low pass, high pass, band pass, notch. From there, at least one phase, one flange filter, one comb filter, sample and hold, and the ring mod. Those are going to be the main ones."

### EP5 - "Envelopes" (m9T_CfPNKKs, 30 min) - subs OK
- Framing: "we're going to be learning about envelopes, which is going to allow us to make punchy bases, pads, lush leads, and sounds that move, that change over time."
- Baseline: "In Serum 2, envelope one's routed to the volume by default"; max volume decided by main volume and oscillator levels. ADSR taught in order: Attack ("how long it takes for us to reach the max value, which with this envelope we can't really move or change"), Slope ("slope is going to allow us to gradually go in or slowly come up and then all of a sudden get to that desired loudness, which can be useful for brassy sounds"), Hold (holds max amplitude after attack - designed for staccato presets: "with the hold I can have it be so that when someone presses the note even for a long time, the hold limits that... I need to make it easy for them to use the sound as intended"), Decay ("decay is also very useful for adding perceived punch"), Sustain, Release ("release... is only going to matter if there's sound to begin with").
- Time entry: envelope stage times can be entered as seconds or musical divisions ("Seconds, too, 1/8, 1/4, 16... whenever I'm trying to create an effect").
- Display interactions: drag up/down on the envelope plot to zoom out / in; there is a "lock feature which locks itself automatically zoom in" (auto-zoom toggle with a good-and-bad caveat); Serum 2 addition - when you highlight and move a modulation it "tells you where you're going from to what" (value readout).
- KEY modulation gesture taught here (used all series): "by clicking here and dragging I can drag this [envelope] to any knob... there's a plus whenever I can drag it somewhere... this blue line appears and this blue line is going to tell us the modulation amount." i.e. drag source onto any knob; blue ring/line = amount, drag to adjust.
- Polarity: modulation can be bipolar or unipolar; "hold option or alt shift-click on that blue little knob and you make it unipolar. You can also go into the matrix and you're going to see here polarity."
- Routed targets taught: volume (env 1), filter cutoff (env 2 - creates plucks and wubs: "the most common things that they would add envelopes to are... a filter cutoff to create plucks"), pitch ("there's a lot of techniques here... I can lower down the sustain to create lasers" - also downlifters, 808 snaps, "hello Chris"), octave range, resonance, wavetable position.
- Workflow session: (1) stacked bass - square sub at -2 octaves + saw -1, both into filter, "set the cutoff point by ear where I still hear the bass how I would want it heard when sustained. And then I'm going to use an envelope now to open it up to a certain amount"; level balance "I want where the saw is influencing the bass more than the square, but the square is still providing that low-end body"; "the identity of this bass will come from how much you open up, by the decay you set, sustain, the resonance"; watch the volume - "don't do this cuz you thin it out too much. But you do want some form of reducement in volume, but not too much." (2) rolling/future-bass bass: "with the basic shapes, if you're making a rolling bass... the important thing is that envelope. Super important because it's going to dictate how your bass sounds." (3) supersaw pad: 8 saws, "switch the algorithm to the super", long release, "let's add another envelope that increases the resonance and brings it down", band-passed detuned layer on top for movement. (4) growl from available blocks: spectral wavetable + envelope to wave position + alt warp PWM + multi filter with peak and notch moving separately + serial F1->F2 with an allpass; sinefold distortion inside oscillators; comb 2. (5) Matrix trick: envelope 3 to global master tuning ("this is something I saw in some videos where I was like, why didn't I think of that... we're going to go from the bottom up. Unipolar, one direction"). (6) sample -> wavetable: load a multisample pan flute then "turn it into a wavetable... let's use 1024" (resynthesize a sample into a 1024-frame wavetable). (7) acid: saw + envelope 2 + high resonance.

### EP6 - "LFO Movement" (LgST5jK5FBE, 32 min) - subs OK
- Framing: the LFO system is why Serum became his main synth: "I had never seen such a freeing LFO where I could just draw shapes and make knobs move in ways that I never thought was imaginable." LFO slots grow as you use them - "let's say you make a sound where you're using all six, it starts to give you even more"; "I think we get a max of 10".
- Gesture: same drag-and-drop modulation as envelopes ("we can drag and drop the LFO to the level of this saw").
- Rate: BPM-synced divisions (1/16, 1/8...) plus trip/dot variants; can switch to Hertz mode for unsynced movement ("whenever I want to modulate something that's not synced to the BPM, or... a pitch drift effect").
- Shape browser submenu categories: Basic (saw down, saw up, sine, square/"assign", triangle...), Rhythmic (user-generated complex shapes - "some people sell presets for these"), Sidechain ("side chain shapes which I think are going to come from the LFO Tool"), Random curve, Random flat.
- Playback direction/modes: Forward / Reverse / Ping pong; grid size control; X and Y axis controls; option+click to snap dots to the grid ("by holding option click, we can have the dots attached to the grid"); slope handle adjustments.
- LFO triggers/modes: Free (keeps flowing across notes - "it's continuing the journey"), Retrig ("you're always starting from the beginning"), Envelope mode (plays once and "it's going to stay wherever that last dot is"); Mono toggle (all voices together vs per-voice LFOs - with mono off, "every voice has its LFO... it sounds like an arp"); loop back point ("I could right-click... I can set loop back point here... we just keep looping in this little circle" - plays once, then loops a region).
- Right-side settings, in his order: Rise (modulation ramps in over time - "play a chord and then you want it to wiggle at the end"), Delay (fully delays start), Smooth (new in Serum 2 - "smoothen out the modulation... round it out"; favorite combo: random/random-flat shape then Smooth to invent wubs), Phase ("decides where we start").
- Drawing tools: coordinate dot system; per-grid-box shapes (flat, slope up, slant down...); expand control to view the LFO larger ("open this up more... get very precise").
- Advanced LFO types ("a lot of new LFO modes... back then we didn't have access to these four"): Path (draw X/Y paths; X and Y route to different knobs; "sounds that sound like they're revolving around your head. X controls the level. Y will control the pan"; ships with fancy preset shapes); Chaos, Rusler, and Sample & Hold (generative; same X/Y system; "I'll be honest with you guys, I don't know what they do... it's going to be crazy hectic"; used for unpredictable "binaural" pads and generative growls). Coordinate points can themselves be modulated ("if you right click you can modulate any of the coordinate points"), and BPM lock can be applied.
- Workflow session: (1) reinvent an iconic sound (deadmau5 LP-18 saw): "I reinvent by just using the same sound but just layering on top of it" - wide wavetable layer an octave up, then "maybe the octave is going to switch. Be generative. Let's use the sample and hold"; (2) reshaped wub: LFO on cutoff, envelope mode to play once, shape squared off, sub added, noise color for crunch; (3) tech house filter sound: band reject + LFO, lower the geyser noise level; (4) modulating an LFO's own rate with an envelope ("one popular thing to modulate would probably be this rate... I could drag it here") for melodic techno; (5) pitch strip: LFO on fine tune, Free mode, lowered amount/speed, duplicated detuned saws; (6) gated choir: multisample choir + LFO gate + LFO 2 micro-modulation on filter ("I also want it to gate a bit... more of a micro modulation with LFO 2"); (7) chaos panning across voices with increased polyphony - "that is one of the coolest effects I've heard."
- Principle: "the most important thing to think about LFOs is constant movement. The difference between envelopes and LFOs... is that LFOs can loop as long as you're holding down a note."

### EP7 - "The Matrix (The Pro Section)" (FxmpF24EUYE, 24 min) - subs OK
- Scope: velocity, note modulation, voicing, macros, the Matrix, auxiliary sources, mod/pitchbend wheels.
- Velocity: explained from MIDI basics ("the harder you press a note, the higher the velocity value"); routes like any modulation source; advised to use moderate amounts ("if I programmed a velocity parameter in a patch, it wouldn't be this drastic... just to have a sense of movement in the sound").
- Matrix UI details: "at the top right of this matrix you can see there's this little arrow we can click and there, by default, is create velo-to-amp assignment" (one-click helper that sets up velocity to amp); each mod has a custom response curve you can draw - "with this graph, what you're going to be able to do is create your own custom curve so that way the velocity reacts the way you want it... by default, this is very gradual, I think the term for that would be considered linear"; squared curve = accent behavior ("below a certain value this is very low, above a certain value you get full openness"). Right-click context menu on a mod: initialize graph, lock the module ("as you move through presets, the velocity module you've set stays"), legato portamento time.
- Note modulation: same panel style as velocity but driven by pitch ("this note, the way I like to think about it is like the key track feature we used in the filter section. The higher you play, the higher the value").
- Voicing section: poly count (voice limit - at low values "I'm borrowing notes... they don't even go through the end of the release"), mono, legato ("if I set legato, when I glide my notes, the envelope doesn't re-trig anymore"), portamento time, "always" (portamento always applied - "really cool for dirty Dutch leads"), "scaled" (portamento time scaled by interval size), curve (portamento contour - "if I'm doing something like acid sounds and I want to mimic a 303, this is where I might play with this"), voice steal priority (newest / oldest / highest / lowest / velocity: "if I wanted to keep... the lowest note, I might choose to make the low ones a priority").
- Macros: "knobs that aren't doing anything until you assign it. And you can assign it to multiple knobs, similar to LFOs and envelopes, but the difference is you control it with this knob"; "In Serum 2, you're going to have a total of eight"; macros can route into macros; bipolar or unipolar; right-click menu: remove all destinations / apply / delete; copy-paste between presets. Worked example: one "uplifter" macro holding pitch + EQ frequency + quality + reverb - "all you have to do now is just modulate this one knob through your DAW."
- Aux sources (the Matrix's right-hand columns): conditioners routed into mods - "the most popular thing I would route there [is] velocity... as I increase the velocity, you can see that the LFO is now allowed to roam higher and higher up"; aux signal can be inverted and has its own response curve; manual notes some sources are only assignable here (named: active voices, note-on values).
- Pitchbend wheel: bend-up range numbers ("if you're making an uplifter, I want to use the pitchbend wheel... you want to pitch up from a fifth... you can put the fifth there"), with mod wheel alongside.
- Matrix itself: shows all modulations; macro reordering by drag ("It doesn't alter anything, it's just in case you want certain macros on top"); "I believe you can have a total of 64 [mod slots] inside of Serum 2"; per-row controls: deactivate button, X to delete, amount, polarity, destination, and an "out" column that "shows you a visual of the modulation"; sort by source / sort by destination; lock so the setup survives preset changes.
- Workflow session: acid bass built from velocity - velocity on amp and decay, accent = "when there's an accent that means that the velocity is going to go up... we're going to add it to the cutoff", mono legato + portamento curve for 303 slides; lesson learned live: "that was a bad idea because now there's way too much control" and "velocity is riding a lot of stuff. So let's maybe ease up a bit."
- Close quote: "so now you know what to do with your velocity, your note, your matrix, how to grab presets and add that touch to them so that you can create movement to the sound and make your tracks feel less static."

### EP8 - "Advanced FX Section" (sGgRwigo7Ag, 52 min) - subs OK
- Access: "the effect section of Serum 2 can be reached by just going here and clicking there" (FX view); left side lists MAIN, BUS 1, BUS 2 lanes.
- FX presets ("rack chains") live here: "we're going to have presets now available for you by clicking here... essentially rack chains" (categories incl. Bus Processing; factory ones he likes: "Seven Skies lead split", "Alice lead", "the Duda"); you can save your own racks; when the section is "getting in the way... you can click in here and it will remove it for you" (get it out of the way while in flow).
- Buses: route from the Mix view ("these buses that you can route stuff to"; "think of a master return tracks in the sense"); confirmed later: "bus one and two will only work when you go to the mixer and you route from here". Routing options per oscillator include none / bus 1 / bus 2 / direct out / main and filters; "you can also right-click here... route to filter two or to the direct out or to the main"; there is a per-oscillator "Envelope 1 on" toggle ("if this oscillator runs through envelope one... otherwise it sounds way too static").
- Effects walked through in his order (right-click to add):
  - Bode (Body): frequency shifter "named after Harold Bode"; controls: mono input (admits he still doesn't know what it does), shift, range (percent of shift range - "the thing that this shifter has that the Ableton one doesn't"), dir/direction (center makes channels opposite = wide), width, a mono delay (feedback up = delay, syncable 1/8 dotted; balance between down/up shifted signal; "you're going to hear the pitch effect on the delay"), blur (smear/chorus/flutter). Usage: "I rarely run it at 100 unless it's experimental sound design."
  - Chorus: "duplicate the saw into four voices. Two will go left, two will go right... rate... depth... feedback at high values gives a very metallic effect... just right [enough]... you get this very nice bee swarm." Filter LP/HP inside the chorus so bass isn't widened ("if you have a bass and you don't want this chorus applied to the low end"); reason to choose chorus over detune: "it sounds more retro... a detuned Juno sound."
  - Compressor: attack ("how fast it takes for the compression to come in... with a higher attack you hear the transient"), release, makeup gain, ratio ("4 to 1... for every 4 dB that goes over the threshold"), threshold, limiter at the far right; multiband mode: green = downward, brown = upwards expansion ("a very squashed sound getting hit from the front and the back"), X-low / X-high crossovers ("whatever is set in between that is considered the mids"), per-band ratio, "you can also modulate these guys."
  - Convolve: convolution reverb "impulse file" concept; size ("more size... stretched out"), tone (filter on the impulse, bright to damp), phase (convolution minimum phase - tighter), pre-delay (beats mode: clap then reverb enters), attack (fades in impulse), decay, damp (low pass the highs), impulse volume. Fun use: "sometimes you can produce interesting growls... characteristics of a... goat."
  - Delay: three modes - high quality toggle ("high quality doesn't always mean good... you can turn it off... for a low-fi effect"), normal / ping pong / tap ("ping pong... the delay is going to play on one side first to create the width, because if they play at the same time, which is what normal does, it's going to collapse into the center"; guidance: "look at your song and see where your delay is going to sit best on the sides if it's not too busy, and down the middle if the sides are way too busy"); feedback ("at high it self-oscillates... it's going to get loud"); an internal filter "controls the tone of the delay itself, not the sound"; mix + level; BPM/MS toggle ("if you wanted a dotted, you can lift this up to dot dot"); width via "offset one of the right or left by a few milliseconds"; MS mode for slap delay "or create your own phaser or comb filter this way."
  - Distortion: 13 types (tube, soft clip, hard clip, diode 1, diode 2, fold, sine fold, zero square, down sample, asym, rectify, X shaper, sine shaper, tape saturation, overdrive, soft saturation - auto-captions run them together); favorites: tube; zero square "just squares everything off... the strongest"; down sample "provides a nice little crunch... slowing down the bit rate... the $1 million bass, like the deadmau5 one"; X shaper lets you "draw in your own distortion... to the left you're going to go to your A and to the right you create the B... we're creating movement in sounds with distortion." Pre-filter section: "there is a filtering section in the distortion here, which we would call it a pre-filter... in pre, we create this sound because we're filtering the saw before it reaches the distortion, similar to us putting an EQ before it"; default low shelf + high shelf, can add bells, and "if I hold clicking and holding alt, you can have as many EQs as you want"; scale-graph caveat ("you're reducing here by 7 dB, but it looks like you're reducing by two or three").
  - Filter effect: same filter set, placed in the chain ("if you distort heavy... and you want to filter there instead").
  - Flanger: depth, rate, feedback, phase; phase is a stereo offset - manual quote: "a setting of 50% represents 180 degrees, meaning that the left and right have opposite frequencies. In this case the flanger sweeps up as on the left while falling on the right."
  - Hyper: "a micro chorus effect... meant to increase the voices and detune them"; rate of detune; retrig ("all the voices that you're creating start in the same position, giving us a stronger sound in the beginning"); where "hyper saws" come from.
  - Dimension: "a pseudo stereo effect consisting of four delay lines summed out of phase and slowly amplitude modulated"; size adds phase delays; width tool he is not fond of ("always thought it sounded a little too eh").
  - Phaser: 4 notches up/down, depth, center frequency, rate, feedback, phase ("create width by having the left side be at a different place than the right").
  - Reverbs: plate ("two-dimensional... usually plates tend to be more in your face, sound more metallic"; width, pre-delay, damp, size = more decay, plus an EQ); hall ("usually more depth... higher size is usually darker, more in the back"; pre-delay, decay, spin); vintage ("low and the high cut... ER size... diffusion A... diffusion B... damp"); marble ("five different modes... almost like a delay and a reverb put together"); basin ("a mono reverb").
  - Splitters: "three in total" - low/high, low/mid/high, mid/side ("you can target each one individually"); crossover control ("with this, we control the crossover, so we can apply effects to the low band and the high band separate of each other"); use e.g. add body only to high band.
  - Utility: "mono the bass... everything below 90 Hz should be mono", width knob, pan knob, utility high pass / low pass, polarity invert (L or L+R), mix, volume.
- Right-click the FX bus area: "lock the effects bus. So, as I go through presets, the effects bus will stay"; also "lock all effects buses" (bus 1 and 2).
- Bus signal-flow nuance: "if I route it through here first, I'm routing the saw sound without the filter, because we're creating a different auxiliary channel... it's also going to the main because we have it routed there."
- Sound design session highlights: res bass (saw + arpeggiator, down-sample distortion, reverb on high end, ping-pong echo "so it doesn't sit on top"); wave-shape bass (C2 at -2, diode distortion, envelope on fine); reese (detune, chorus, EQ, OTT/multiband, phaser, mono legato); evolving lead using Body - "signal flow is very important. We can move the effects like so"; EDM supersaw lead (LFO, soft saturation, tape; caution: "too much distortion cuz of the lingering release when they overlap"); gated lead; offbeat bass (sine LFO on level, alt-click copies the shape); kick+bass bus split - 909 kick sample triggered per quarter, "now bus one is the bass... we have the kick in bus two. And if I want to process everything together I can do it in the main"; melodic techno stab (analog "Matrix 664" wavetable, envelope 3, unison, sinefold/sine shaper, pre-EQ, hall reverb + delay).
- Quotes: "signal flow is very important."; "sometimes with the EQ you might have to do crazy boost. It's more of a sound design thing cuz you're trying to get a certain part of the sound out."; "the key for me is always to get everything to sound like this, but to get this [next level]... takes a little bit of time and effort."

### EP9 - "FM Warp" (q1F82VUo4GY, 26 min) - subs OK
- Scope: the advanced modulations at the bottom of the Warp menu: "today we're getting into Serum 2's FM section, which you're going to access by clicking the warp and going below distortion, where you're going to find a lot of modulations like FM... PD, which is the old serum FM, known as phase distortion, AM, which is amplitude modulation... and then ring modulation, RM."
- Sources: "you're going to be able to route multiple different modulation sources. Usually in this scenario it's going to be either the oscillator B/C, the filter outputs, sub oscillator and even the noise." Serum 2 addition: self-routing - "its own self now, which back then you couldn't do... I'm going to assume this is a feedback because in some FM sounds, to create the iconic saw sound like the lately bass, it would have to feed back into itself." So the warp menu has a source picker incl. self.
- FM behavior: through-zero toggle ("by default we have through zero activated down here"; manual quote: keeps "the carrier oscillator... to continue to oscillate correctly even when its frequency is modulated into negative values"; his take: "true zero just really is going to be the cleaner one... relatively stays more in key"); ratio math taught via Pitch Mode: right-click the pitch "mode" -> Harmonics / Ratio ("ratio, which is what most FM synthesizers that we know of out there use"), then a "Source" selector ("I want to go source and pick the oscillator that's going to be producing the sound... oscillator A... if I'm playing a C and I put the ratio of two, I'm going to have this guy be an octave above. If I put it at three, we're now on the fifth").
- Alternative curves: Through-zero vs Exponential vs Linear; exponential "starts off similar to a linear but then it starts to go faster and faster... leads to the FM sounding a lot more drastic"; manual calls linear "smooth, clean and more musical... great for bell-like tones" but he finds "true zero is the one that keeps its key a lot better"; the linear/exponential cross-mod "is the kind you'll find like on a Jupiter 6 or Jupiter 8... this cross mod one... sounds exactly like it."
- PD vs FM: "if you like the sounds most people were making with serum one when they did FM on there, then usually you want to go with the PD, the phase distortion, over the traditional FM"; PD also accepts the extra sources.
- AM: "similar to FM except the amplitude, the volume is modulated... it's actual volume automation... eventually... it's moving so fast that it produces overtones."
- RM: "multiplication of both of these guys... at low values it provides movement to a sound. But at high volumes... you start to create instability... making it sound more aonal... good for sound design of drums... techno... metallic objects... a hollow sound"; explains sum + difference frequencies not harmonically related; manual doesn't cover it well.
- FM/AM on samples: "Serum 2 allows you to actually FM sounds like, for instance, sampled bass sounds" (works with the sample/multisample engines).
- Envelope on FM: "using an envelope on the FM is very common in FM synthesis. Sometimes you want that tone, but you don't want it forever. So this is when you would use an envelope."
- Sub doctrine (motivated by FM sounds being hard to EQ): "use a sub when you have a sound that you like the tone of, but it's going to be impossible to mix lowend into it... you avoid [ringing frequencies and phase shifts from extreme EQ] by using a sine wave as your sub"; on cancellation: "phase cancellation... is relative to volume. So... if the subs in this sound aren't as loud as the sub I'm about to put, there's low risk of canceling out."
- Sound design: deep house bass (PD + "the FM can be modulated... route envelope 2... open up and then come back to a starting position to give us a nice punchy deep houseish"; plus "slap delay... very iconic of back in the day... EDX"; pitch envelope technique); botanical pluck ("they would use a lot of combs to get this sounding like this" - Equinox Sounds botanical pack reference; conga click layer; "I am going to add OTT... might turn into a slap house bass"; convolution reverb for the botanical feel; key track the note).
- Quotes: "reverb... it's a crutch in the sense that... it makes anything sound good"; "if you want to make precise sounds, always have a strategy when you're doing sound design."

### EP10 - "Clips & Arps" (TY6FRwAb0YQ, 22 min) - subs OK
- Purpose of Clip mode: "Clip mode, for me, is an opportunity to show everyone that uses my sounds how the sounds are intended to be used" (preset authoring / demo clips). Skeptical intro: "why do we need a clip mode inside of Serum 2?": he demystifies it.
- Access: "you're going to access the clip section bottom left here by right clicking. You can lock it... but also MIDI input, trigger, octave." Bottom keyboard range convention: "after a certain octave range... everything you play down there starts to sound... too low for any comprehension of tonality... programs like Kontakt... use the bottom section to switch between different playing modes... in Serum 2, those bottom ones, like my C negative 2, is going to switch between the different clips you have and between the different arps you have."
- Banks: "you can create banks for yourself. You can save clip banks... factory banks like the Duda chords, Neo chords."
- Trigger mode: mono or poly - "can you play more than one clip at the same time?"; Edit-All toggle: "edit all of the clips found here with these settings."
- Clip settings: Length ("how long your intended clip is going to be"); Keyboard span (transpose/play the clip from the keyboard); Offset ("each note that I play is going to make it start at a different section... a cool way to kind of play a clip, you know, like randomizing"); on randomization: "some people will record themselves playing and then randomize the way it plays... these are all ways and strategies of breaking the habits."
- Playback modes: Normal, Reverse, Pendulum ("hit the end and then reverse into itself"), Random, Random Note Duplication, Random Start, Random Ending, One Shot, and Static ("only play the first note combination... the chord banks are all set to static... that way the clip isn't moving to the right and then you lose the chord"). Plus time-signature divisions, Speed (rate, triplets, dotted), Quantization on Launch, Re-Trig / Velocity Re-Trig ("every time we switch a note, how is this clip going to react").
- Editing workflow: he dislikes Step input ("I hate the system personally"), so: "I'll record myself in Ableton... then after I've recorded myself, I'll just hit record here and play it out"; then shortcuts - "command A, command Q, which is going to sync it up" (select all + quantize; "we can quantize with command Q, we can reverse with command R"), scale-time "50 to 200%"; right-click menu: "we can conform to a scale... Command L"; Overdub ("record... and you're going to see the macros changing down there" - automation capture); Extend ("when you reach the end it continues further"); Metronome toggle; zoom in/out; "you're going to find all of your little automations down here."
- Arp: shape selector ("by default usually up, but we can go between a lot of them"); speed + subdivisions (triplets, dotted, unsync option); NOTE: "these guys will be modulable by envelopes and LFOs as well on certain parameters" (arp parameters are modulation destinations); Transposition section ("one of my favorite, most underused sections... after all the notes are played, this will get transposed up by a semitone"; set to 12 + range 2 for octave-running patterns - "people like Flume would use them in these crazy ways"); Latch ("let go and it will just continue playing"); MIDI-thru; Offset ("instead of playing C... shift it to the right"); Repeats ("it only repeats twice and then it stops"); Gate ("controls the length of each note"); Chance ("the probability of the notes playing"); Re-Trigger; Velocity mode ("it comes down... it's working its way down to the targeted velocity, then it stays there").
- Pattern mode - the hidden gem: "one of the most hidden sections that is insane in Serum 2... worth its money"; clicking here opens the pattern editor with rate 1x; the pattern rows map to chord note indices ("we can say three to five notes... zero is C... the D# is a two note... so you can create a custom arp so it doesn't sound that repetitive"); Accents row "gives us access to essentially like acid style patterns... it's going to make the velocity jump"; Wrap handles out-of-range notes; offset and speed work here too; velocity can also be routed to decay etc.
- MIDI out (bottom right): "command shift T to open up a new channel... record this" - lets the incoming notes be transposed/output (chord inversion demo); Clip-player vs arp: "if I set clip player on, it's only going to play the stuff from the clip and it won't incorporate the arp into it. But if I set it on, it's going to incorporate the arp" (toggle deciding whether arp feeds the clip output).
- Keyboard option: scale quantizer ("if I set this to, let's say, D minor... it's going to shift all the notes that I'm playing that aren't part of that scale into the scale"); Swing applied to arp and clip; transposition per key.
- Oscillator mapping: limits each oscillator to a keyboard range - "you kind of know what kind of music you want to make, or you want to create a patch that someone with a long keyboard can use, or they can create essentially a bass and a lead at the same time"; bass C0-C2 on osc A, lead above on osc B, each routed to its own filter; critical caveat: if osc B only warps osc A, "you're not going to hear it do anything because this guy is not playing at all until it hits the top one. So if you set warp on, it will make it so that no matter if it's playing or not, you're still applying the FM/warp."
- Preset UX: "right-click on this guy and set as preview clip. So now when you click on this little play button, it's going to show you the example of how... what you recorded in there."
- Close: "the ARP section is insane. It's one of the hidden gems no one's really talking about."

### EP11 - "Create Your Own Wavetables" (coz9O7YBky0, 34 min) - subs OK
- Access & purpose: "the way to access the wavetable editor... you go to the saw, top right... that little pencil button. Now, the purpose of the wavetable editor is to create your own wave tables, which, as we already know, is the color of your sound." Also used to "create custom morphs, custom tables with multiple subtables... up to nine for this whole wave table. In order to morph between them, or to provide yourself or your users... a certain color palette."
- Editing model: the editor is harmonic-bin based - "at the very top... all these bins... related to the harmonics, the frequency of the sound. At the very beginning we have bin one, which is my fundamental"; gray outlines mark octave harmonics; the lower half is "the relationship on phase for each harmonic"; you can draw curves (brush settings), pick a grid of built-in shapes ("select the grid of 101 which is just going to input the shape 101... made a saw like that"), or enter FORMULAS (flagship presets like "Michelangelo waves", "Fibonacci" - "just math, math, math").
- Right-click generators: generate saw, randomize top / bottom / all, clear, progressive fade, shift octave up/down, repeat bin group, draw-even-harmonics-only, draw-odd-harmonics-only ("more of a square type of sound"), and a "scale frequency values by bin index" view toggle that he keeps on ("it doesn't make it look so tiny").
- Per-frame processes (right side list): normalize ("make the amplitude of that wave at least hit the ceiling"), remove DC offset, flip polarity vertical/horizontal, shift horizontal zero crossing, fade in edges, x-fade edges, filter, sample redux + grid size ("square it... lower quality"), send to noise oscillator. (Fun extra: "we can grab wave tables and turn them to LFO shapes" - wavetable -> LFO shape conversion.)
- All-frames processes: normalize each gain separately / all / between; remove fundamental ("very useful when you're making baselines... so that you don't have a low end that's fluctuating in volume, beating"); remove low spectra; remove low phases; sample redux; "resize tables to half the number" (creates new tables from each, "you make the most out of each one"); create PWM from selected frame ("shift of the middle to the left... adding movement"); set spectra frame to all; set phases frame to all; subtract spectra from other oscillators; blur.
- Frame management: "remove all except selected" via right-click, remove beginnings/ends, select multiple to remove, reduce waveform.
- Morph section (the payoff): "the morph section, which is the more important section... this section is what's going to allow you to morph these three to create a full out wave table with 256 essentially images to it" - crossfade ("now I'm at 256, which is the max"), spectral morph, zero fundamental phase, zero all phases; the palette metaphor ("the sky palette, right? light blue, purple, orange and yellow - and that's the palette, that's the wave table").
- Workflow technique - building tables from rendered warps: "I can go to the menu and I can resample... render oscillator warp A... so now that shape that we had there is here. So I can copy that... paste" - he renders a warp (e.g. FM/PD) into a fixed waveform, copies it into the editor as a new subtable, and iterates: "Since we have an oscillator C, I'm going to use C... to drop all the tones I'm going to create" (clipboard/oscillator as scratch space). Also from EP5: sample -> wavetable via "turn it into a wavetable... use 1024".
- Uses & experiments: organ bass tables from bins around the fundamental; layering custom tables; "remove the fundamental" for bass; final sound-design pass with alt warps, matrix bipolar mods, phasers, flange combs, subs + OTT to finish the table-based patch.
- Quotes: "Creating wave tables is an art in its own, as you can see."; "to become an expert at the wavetable editor, you got to know how to input formulas and math."

### EP12 - "Global Section" (D2GB6bGy-Nw, 14 min) - subs OK
- Section purpose: "the global section of Serum 2, which is going to give us access to a couple of important features. One, workflow things that we can turn on or off."
- Workflow toggles he walks through (great UX research material):
  - Help tooltips ("like when I hover over stuff, it will tell me... the description") - can be turned off.
  - Param value tooltips (similar).
  - Double-click pattern: Reset vs "type value" - "if I have something like the tune up and I want to put it back to its default position, if I double click it does that. Versus if I put type value, it allows me to input like a value and it will set it to that value."
  - Mouse wheel parameter control: "if I have a trackpad and I want to move up with the trackpad or the mouse wheel, then you can also do that. And you can also use a ball in a circle, like circular motions... which I leave on... super clutch", with the caveat that accidental movement is why you might turn it off.
  - Keyboard shortcuts (command-undo handling) - change if a DAW shortcut conflicts.
  - Default waveform view: 2D or 3D - "if I put this in 3D, you're going to see nothing really happens right now until I initialize the preset. Then everything pops up in 3D, which I personally choose to have off" (needs a preset re-init to take effect; he disables it).
  - MPE activation; "mod wheel to wavetable position when wavetable editor is open" (credits it as "super clutch" but reports it not working for him); "silence not effects tells when host transport stops" (kills reverb tails when the host stops; can feel unnatural); "use ultra quality when rendering" ("you can run this in good mode, but when you actually render the track, it switches to ultra for you, which I leave on"); auto check for updates; auto-delete renders after 30 days (renders = resampled oscillator warps etc.).
- Voice control section (the sound-design part of Global): "this is going to allow us to really change every single note that hits slightly... every time a new voice is set, a new note, we can add slight variations to each note, which makes the sound come alive... it has more bounce, versus, oh, it's very static sounding."
  - Pan spread example from hardware: Dave Smith synths - "every time a new note would hit, it would either be pan left or right... you might find a preset that does this... it's literally just an auto pan."
  - Detune section: "you get the drift... for humanizing a sound, adding more movement" - an alternative to free-running LFO volume modulation ("after every note hits, another system of doing it... super clutch because it's one of the new ones").
  - Randomize on the left side ("if you don't want to go in and do this to, let's say, your pad's tune, cutoff, envelopes, modulation percentages, then you can choose to just randomize it here").
  - Scaling (up/down "dependent on our envelopes... we're multiplying or decreasing the values") with visual feedback: "you can see there's this yellow asterisk that appears to let us know that there is some form of change going on with the scaling of it. Same thing for LFOs and same thing for the rate, the speed of the LFOs."
  - Factory presets exist for voice control to play with.
- Voice map section (per-note modulation of envelope stages, "similar to what Diva will have"): "the percentage goes up, this goes down... it's going to change the values of the decay, sustain, release" for each voice.
- Right side: quality mode (with Serum 1 compatibility mode for old presets; disable smoothing option - "why would I want to do that? But maybe you might save some CPU"); tuning reference ("I've never understood it... most synths are tuned to 440").
- Preset browser section (advanced preset options):
  - Randomize preset from the selected library/folder ("I like to use this whenever I'm working on a song... and I really don't know what I want... it gets me out of the comfort zone and into divisions/folders I usually tend to avoid").
  - Hybridize presets: "combining the presets and making like a new sort of preset... hybridize favoring selected presets."
  - Delete / rename / move / autoplay previews ("as I go through them it just kind of plays them, so you don't have to hit the play button").
  - Tags via right-click; his UX critique: "it's just kind of redundant... I have to scroll through all the ones I've created... there should probably be a system where I should be able to double click and just type and it will give me what I want... like suggested as I'm typing it out" (wants type-to-search with suggestions).
  - Notes; categories; category sidebar (pads, lead, hit, stab...) driven by tags and ratings.
- Close: goal is "make the most out of your preset browser. Randomize, hybridize presets together. Rate your presets, tag your presets. You should be able to apply the voice map section to add a bit of humanization to the sound."

### EP13 (standalone) - "I Stole a Trick From a Legendary Synth" (lOZ56pKhTqU, 10 min) - subs OK (en-orig track)
- Concept: recreate a Chris Stussy-style organic house flute by copying the Roland JV-1080 philosophy - "combined sampled instrument tones like this, like a pan flute, while at the same time creating like a synthetic version of it and filtering them together. So this inspiration came from that philosophy that they used."
- Steps in order:
  1. Load the organic source in Sample/Multisample: "we can now go into a multi-sample or sample feature. I think sample would be the better bet if you're trying to sound a little bit more old-school"; flute > pan flute.
  2. Humanize with envelope 1: "go into envelope one and add a bit of attack because a real flute... someone's going to have to breathe and blow into it. And also release to kind of allow there to be a tail"; "let's lower the sustain a bit". Pacing note: "with sound design, take your time because a lot of the creation of the sounds, one simple turn can just mess everything up."
  3. THE STOLEN TRICK - sample -> wavetable conversion: "click alt, drag it here, and then from there click here and you can switch this to a wavetable. Now what I want to use is the FFT 256, 512, 1024 and 2048. What this does is it breaks down the sound into frequency ingredients, and the higher the number, the more pictures Serum 2 is going to take... a higher number will give you more detail... a lot smoother"; he picks 256 because the goal is a single static tone, not scanning ("the Roland JV-1080 didn't do this").
  4. Wavetable editor cleanup: "I would like to go to the wavetable editor and I will hit all and I will normalize each gain separately. And from there, I will find one that I like." (Uses one chosen frame.)
  5. Synthetic layer: "hit the unison up and detune... if you've ever used an old-school wavetable synth, it sounds very retro. This is going to be like a synthetic layer."
  6. Filter the synthetic layer back: "the key thing is you want to use a filter to remove all of the top end of that sound which sounds very synthetic... this wavetable moves more to the back and it acts as a layer to fill up the flute." Summary: "that's how we create this organic sound and just beef it up with synthetic waves where we kind of still keep that naturalness in it."
- FX: reverb, prefer factory presets as starting points; "vintage hall" for a vintage vibe; ping-pong delay 1/8 dotted ("Chris... likes to use these echoes a lot... 1/8 dotted just puts the 1/8 at more of a swingier vibe"); EQ to make the highs less shimmery.
- Macro pluck technique: "if I wanted to pluck it up, usually what I'll do is I'll grab a macro and I will pull back the attack on the sound. Lower down the sustain and the decay as well... we don't want to make it too plucky cuz then it loses all the flavor."
- Pad variant: "set a forward and reverse loop here... key thing many people will forget is... we can select here to create a fade. So, as it comes in and out, it's done smoother" (loop crossfade); octave-up option; high-pass filter with a note that "the bottom warp here makes the filter more gradual rather than instant change".
- Glue: compressor "2:1 ratio to glue it together", attack ~30, longer release ("the longer the release, the slower the compressor moves... making it more of a musical compressor over a knocker"); optional flanger "to make it feel more nostalgic".
- Takeaway: "start with an organic layer. Could be a guitar, could be a flute, it could be a saxophone. And from there, you create a synthetic layer by creating a wavetable out of it that you're going to keep static. You're not really going to scan through."

### EP14 (standalone) - "How Pros Make WIDE Bass" (iF8cm3RmVmQ, 9 min) - subs OK (en-orig track)
- Goal: "create a wide bassline that is mono compatible... anybody can sound wide, but only a select few people, producers, can sound good wide in a little boom box speaker"; design for both headphone listeners and "the beach listeners".
- Step 1 - foundation: "the first thing you want to create is the foundation, which is going to be the low end part of your bass. For this, I like to either use a sine or... a saw or a square filtered"; filter the highs off; inspect harmonic spread with an EQ ("I like to kind of think of it as a jigsaw puzzle... make sure we're not invading the space of the center one").
- Step 2 - wide top layers (osc B/C): lock phase first ("the first thing is I'm going to lock the phases so that I can control where it starts every single time"); duplicate the layer ("hold alt, drop it there"); "pan hard left and right on both of these"; then "the big important one is that we can control the phase."
- Measurement discipline: uses a stereo imager - "anything above zero means mono-compatible"; "what we're trying to avoid is going below zero a lot and going to minus one, which is a place no producer should ever be at, unless it's a pad or a supersaw"; mono-check the bass: "add a mono or a utility where you can mono the sound to hear how the people at the beach are going to hear it."
- Beating theory: "if your sub, your bass is at minus two, don't have other oscillators... interacting at that bottom one with it, because you get something known as beating... which makes the reese what it is... however, for a bass like this, we don't really want it."
- Bus routing usage: route the wide layers so they pass through Serum's bus system - "if we go into the mix section, we now have access in Serum 2 to these buses on the right... very valuable for parallel buses, meaning like auxiliary channels that you can send the sound to, but still have the sound going to the masters"; filters set to "none" so the path doesn't double up.
- Safety net at the table editor level: "click the little pencil icon [wavetable editor] and you can go all and remove the fundamental... that's going to make it so that the sub will always remain there, no matter what."
- The clean / sound-designer method: "the only way to get proper width where it's fully at plus one, plus one, is to have two different tonal sounds on the left and the right. Because if they're both the same, they're going to collapse down the center." Example: hard-pan one layer left and give the other side a different character (e.g. PWM); keep them "kind of in the same tonal frequency"; then "balance the levels because the louder side's going to present itself more."
- One-sub rule: "the proper way that I learned from a good, prolific sound designer, Rob Papen: always just have one sub oscillator at minus two... and never have any other one if it's a bass."
- Closing: "if I made your production session a little bit more funner today, my goal is accomplished."

## PART 2 - EDMProd guide digest

Source: https://www.edmprod.com/serum-2-guide/ ("Serum 2 Tutorial: The Ultimate Guide for Beginners (2025)", Simon Haven). Article sections: Pricing; Interface; Components; Oscillator View; Mix View; FX View; Matrix View; Global View; Modulations (Envelopes, LFOs); Clip Sequencer and Arpeggiator.

### Interface (layout described in prose - most valuable part for the redesign)
- "Although it might be a bit overwhelming at first, Serum 2's interface is actually really well organized." The article numbers regions on a screenshot:
  - #1 The Views: "Serum 2 has 5 views you can switch between. The view you pick will then be displayed in the main view (number 2)." Views = Osc (default on startup), Mix, FX, Matrix, Global.
  - #2 Main View: displays whichever view is selected (a shared canvas that all 5 views render into).
  - #3 Macros: one-knob control of several parameters; called "one of the most underutilised workflow hacks in music production."
  - #4 Envelopes: draw custom envelopes and apply them to specific parameters; "by default, envelope 1 is assigned to the master volume. It therefore acts as your basic ADSR envelope."
  - #5 LFOs: draw custom LFO curves and apply them.
  - Other areas: "Velocity and Note modulation (bottom-right) let you modulate parameters based on how hard you play a note (Velocity) or the pitch of the note (Note)... you could assign Note to the panning of an oscillator: a low note will now be panned left while higher notes will be panned right." Clip sequencer = "integrated piano roll"; Arpeggiator.
- Disabled-state affordance: "different sections at the top are greyed-out. That is because those functionalities are disabled at the moment."
- Osc view contents: "3 main oscillators, the sub oscillator (all the way on the left), the noise oscillator, and the 2 filters."

### Oscillator View
- "Serum 2... remains a wavetable synthesizer (although Xfer now brands it as an advanced hybrid synthesizer). This means it uses morphing oscillators to generate sound."
- Third oscillator: "you can use OSC B to modulate OSC A, and then add OSC C to thicken up the sound!"
- Five oscillator engines: Wavetable / Multisample / Sample / Granular / Spectral.
  - Wavetable: "load a wavetable, then scroll through the different frames using the WT POS knob"; custom wavetables via a folder (Xfer Records > Serum 2 Presets > Tables).
  - Multisample: "play Serum like a multi-sampled instrument (similar to Kontakt libraries)"; loads the open-source .sfz format; "a collection of samples, with each sample being assigned to a different keyboard note"; doubles as a drum sampler via "Drums" libraries.
  - Sample: "set your start and end points, switch between multiple play modes (one-shot, forward loop, reverse loop etc.)".
  - Granular: "cutting a sample into various grains and then playing them back... control the size (i.e., length) of the grains, the space between grains... Density (i.e. number) of grains; Length of each grain; Randomization of play direction, pitch, length...".
  - Spectral: "re-synthesizes the frequency spectrum, with various controls for time and pitch... you get to import images directly into it (a bit like FL Studio's Harmor)."

### Mix View
- "a fully integrated mixer, one of the first times I've seen this in a synth"; "a great addition to get a bird's eye view of what is happening in Serum."
- Shows: which oscillators are on or off; "where they are routed to (filter A or B or a blend of the 2, directly to the Out channel, etc.)"; which filters are active and "on what mode (low-pass, high-pass...)"; "the list of effects active in the main channel, Bus 1 or Bus 2."
- Actions: "you can change any of these routings, turn oscillators on or off, turn their gain up or down directly within the Mixer view."
- Limitation called out: reordering effects is NOT possible here - "You cannot drag and drop these effects to re-arrange their order, you need to go in the FX view for that"; you can deactivate individual effects via a small "bypass" icon.

### FX View
- "you can now stack up the same effect multiple times, which was impossible before Serum 2"; duplication gesture: "hold Option on Mac or Alt on Windows and drag the effect. That will create a copy of the effect with the same parameters."
- New effects: Bode (frequency shifter), Convolve (convolution reverb), Utility, plus new modes like Overdrive in Distortion.
- Routing: "3 different lanes... MAIN, BUS 1, and BUS 2... lets you create completely different chains of effects. You can decide to send OSC 1 to BUS 1... and OSC 2 to BUS 2" and "send a certain amount of an oscillator to each BUS" (example: ~24% of OSC C to BUS 1, 60% to BUS 2).

### Matrix View
- "view and fine-tune all your modulations"; e.g. see that "Envelope 1 is controlling the panning of OSC A; Envelope 2 is controlling the blend of voices of OSC B; LFO 1 is controlling the frequency cutoff of Filter 1."
- Actions: "adjust the amount of modulation by moving the sliders left and right, change the source or destination of a given modulation, or even set up new modulation"; helps "identify any weird effects that are happening in your sound, but you can't quite locate what the cause is"; bypass a modulation "by clicking on the arrow all the way on the right."

### Global View
- Mostly set-and-forget: "sound quality; MPE settings; Mod wheel options; default waveform view (2D or 3D); and more."
- Voice control section: "make subtle changes to the panning, pitch, filter cutoff, and more for up to 8 notes played consecutively... It's almost like you're creating a pattern, but for the panning of each note" - same idea works for detuning to add variation.

### Modulations
- Envelopes: 4 envelopes; ENV 1 = synth level output (the ADSR); new in Serum 2: a BPM option at the bottom right - "switch between BPM and MS. Choosing BPM will let you sync your envelope with the BPM of your project. For example, you could have the attack stage rise up for precisely 1 beat, and a sustain phase lasting for exactly 2 beats."
- LFOs: "up to 10 LFOs available; chaos modes for absolutely wild effects; an LFO drawing tool to design custom LFO shapes; ability to save presets."

### Clip Sequencer and Arpeggiator
- Clip sequencer = "a piano roll" inside Serum: "12 different banks (slots) where you can create different sequences; set loop markers within your sequence; portamento curve."
- Trigger pattern (explicit workflow): "make sure the clip sequencer is turned on (via the on/off button). Then... right-click on the word CLIP > MIDI input trigger octave > select '1'. Now, when you press C1, Serum will play Clip 1. If you press C#1, it will play Clip 2."
- Arpeggiator: "type of pattern (upward, downward etc.), the rate of play, the number of octaves"; "ARP slots with different patterns, which you can trigger with your MIDI keyboard; a pattern editor lets you create your own arpeggiator patterns."
- "You can combine the Clip Sequencer and the Arpeggiator by turning both on."

## Workflow expectations captured (consolidated)

The strongest workflow/UX lessons for the Anvil redesign, each attributed to its source. (EP = video episode in Part 1; Guide = EDMProd section in Part 2.)

1. One window, five view tabs. Structure the synth around 5 top-level views (Osc - default on open, Mix, FX, Matrix, Global), all rendered into one shared main area; greyed-out sections at the top signal features that are disabled in the current state. (Guide - Interface/Components)
2. Drag-to-modulate is the core gesture of the whole instrument. Drag any source (envelope, LFO, macro, velocity, note) onto ANY knob; show the amount as a ring/line overlay that is itself draggable; option/alt+shift-click flips unipolar/bipolar; the same assignment appears as a row in the Matrix. (EP5 - "by clicking here and dragging I can drag this to any knob"; EP7; Guide - Matrix View)
3. The Matrix is the cockpit, not a hidden table. Rows = source -> destination with amount and polarity; per-row deactivate and delete; sort by source / destination; a visual "out" column; "auxiliary" conditioner sources (velocity, note); lock the setup so it survives preset changes; a one-click helper can create common assignments ("create velo-to-amp"). (EP7; Guide - Matrix View)
4. Right-click is the second layer of the UI. Expert options live behind context menus directly on controls: smooth interpolation on WT POS, pitch mode harmonics/ratio, snap/normalize/reverse/trim on samples, loop options, "show XY controller", LFO loop-back point, wavetable-editor transforms, "set as preview clip". (EP1, EP2, EP3, EP6, EP10, EP11)
5. The oscillator display is a control, not a readout. Click it to open the wavetable browser; the same click-point switches the engine (Wavetable / Multisample / Sample / Granular / Spectral). (EP2 - "you just click on the wave table and then you get the submenu"; Guide - Oscillator View)
6. Tone-first wavetable browsing. Category menus (Analog / Digital / Spectral / User) let users hunt by color; a static wavetable position is a legitimate "tone selector" - not every patch needs scanning. (EP1)
7. Sample engines must be full citizens. Give Sample / Multisample the same polish: start/end/loop markers with snapping, slice markers (option+click adds), root note, scan-rate and BPM locks, normalize/reverse/trim in context, velocity layers. (EP2)
8. Two filters with routing baked into the UI. Route buttons on the filters (highlight = enabled), series vs parallel chains, a mirror control near the oscillator ("filter balance"), slope picker (6/12/18/24), keytrack, and a deep library of filter flavors that "matters a ton". (EP4 - "when it's highlighted blue, it's telling Serum that the sound is being allowed through"; Guide - Mix View)
9. Mix view = bird's-eye routing map. Show on/off state, per-oscillator filter targets, filter modes, and the FX chain per lane; allow toggling, gain and routing edits there; keep FX reordering in the FX view (accepted division of labor - "you need to go in the FX view for that"). (Guide - Mix View, FX View)
10. FX lanes (Main / Bus 1 / Bus 2) with per-oscillator sends. Parallel processing as a first-class feature (bass on bus 1, kick on bus 2, glue on main) with lockable bus racks. (EP8; EP14; Guide - FX View)
11. FX chain editing gestures: drag to reorder ("signal flow is very important"), option/alt-drag to duplicate an effect with the same parameters, save whole chains as presets, stack the same effect repeatedly. (EP8; Guide - FX View)
12. Envelope discipline. Env 1 = amp by default; stage times enterable in seconds or note divisions; zoom and lock in the display; a Hold stage for staccato preset design; slope for brass-like onsets; live value readout while dragging mods. (EP5; Guide - Modulations)
13. LFO superset. Many slots (up to 10, list grows as you use them); drawable shapes with grid snap (option+click), rise / delay / smooth / phase controls, free / retrig / envelope playback, mono-vs-per-voice, random and sample-and-hold generators, plus "smooth" to sculpt random shapes into wubs. (EP6; Guide - LFOs)
14. "Constant movement" principle. LFOs loop while a note is held; envelopes fire once - and an LFO in envelope mode becomes a custom one-shot shaper. Presets should feel alive, not static. (EP6)
15. Velocity and Note are first-class modulators with drawable response curves (linear vs squared=accent) and quick-create actions; lockable across presets. (EP7)
16. The voicing panel matters: poly limit, mono/legato behavior (whether gliding re-triggers envelopes), portamento time / always / scaled / curve, and voice-steal priority (newest/oldest/highest/lowest/velocity) as exposed controls. (EP7)
17. Macros: 8 knobs, multi-destination, macros-to-macros, bipolar; treat them as the "one-knob" story preset users depend on (the uplifter macro example). (EP7; Guide - Macros)
18. Global = pro setup. Tooltips on/off, double-click behavior (reset vs type-value), mouse-wheel and circular-gesture parameter control, 2D/3D default waveform view (applies on preset re-init), ultra quality when rendering, auto-delete renders after 30 days. (EP12; Guide - Global View)
19. Humanize at the voice level. Per-note pan spread, detune drift and randomize; a voice-map for per-note envelope variation; a visible yellow asterisk when scaling is active. (EP12; Guide - Global View)
20. Clips and Arp live inside the synth with a keyboard-access convention: low octaves switch clips/arps (Kontakt-style keyswitches); Static clip mode for chords; a pattern editor with accents; swing; scale quantize; "set as preview clip" for preset demos; arp parameters are modulation destinations. (EP10; Guide - Clip Sequencer and Arpeggiator)
21. Oscillator mapping for playable splits: constrain each oscillator to a note range (bass below C2 on A, lead above on B) so one instance plays like two instruments; mind the "warp even when the osc is muted" nuance. (EP10)
22. The preset browser is a creative tool: randomize-from-folder, hybridize presets, autoplay previews, tags/categories/ratings. The presenter explicitly asks for type-to-search with suggestions instead of tag-scrolling. (EP12)
23. Rendered/resampled material is raw material: sample->wavetable conversion with FFT size choice (256-2048), rendering warps into static waves, wavetable-editor transforms (normalize each frame, remove fundamental, fade edges), morph to 256 frames. "Remove fundamental" = guaranteed-safe layering. (EP5; EP11; EP13; EP14)
24. Layering doctrine: organic + synthetic layer pairs; fill what the other layer misses; ONE sub only (Rob Papen rule) with a sine sub when low end can't be EQed in; modest randomization/unison amounts; measure (imager / mono-check) instead of guessing. (EP2, EP9, EP13, EP14)
25. Workflow psychology the series instills: "stay in flow. Move fast" (know the toolset); "with sound design, take your time... one simple turn can mess everything up"; build knowledge as blocks and immediately use each block alone before combining them (the series' pedagogy: learn a section, then a sound-design session restricted to that section). (EP1, EP2, EP13)
